claim: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides.
source: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides, a reaction that is essential for DNA biosynthesis and repair.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the function of RNR.

claim: The conversion of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides by RNR is essential for DNA biosynthesis and repair.
source: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides, a reaction that is essential for DNA biosynthesis and repair.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of the enzyme.

claim: RNR is responsible for reducing all four ribonucleotide substrates.
source: This enzyme is responsible for reducing all four ribonucleotide substrates, with specificity regulated by the binding of an effector to a distal allosteric site.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characteristic of RNR.

claim: Specificity of RNR for different substrates is regulated by the binding of an effector to a distal allosteric site.
source: This enzyme is responsible for reducing all four ribonucleotide substrates, with specificity regulated by the binding of an effector to a distal allosteric site.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a mechanism of regulation.

claim: In all characterized RNRs, the binding of effector dATP alters the active site to select for pyrimidines over purines.
source: In all characterized RNRs, the binding of effector dATP alters the active site to select for pyrimidines over purines, whereas effectors dGTP and TTP select for substrates ADP and GDP, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a general property of characterized RNRs based on prior knowledge.

claim: Effector dGTP selects for substrate ADP in RNRs.
source: In all characterized RNRs, the binding of effector dATP alters the active site to select for pyrimidines over purines, whereas effectors dGTP and TTP select for substrates ADP and GDP, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a general property of characterized RNRs.

claim: Effector TTP selects for substrate GDP in RNRs.
source: In all characterized RNRs, the binding of effector dATP alters the active site to select for pyrimidines over purines, whereas effectors dGTP and TTP select for substrates ADP and GDP, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a general property of characterized RNRs.

claim: Structures of Escherichia coli class Ia RNR with all four substrate/specificity effector-pairs bound (CDP/dATP, UDP/dATP, ADP/dGTP, GDP/TTP) have been determined.
source: Here, we have determined structures of Escherichia coli class Ia RNR with all four substrate/specificity effector-pairs bound (CDP/dATP, UDP/dATP, ADP/dGTP, GDP/TTP) that reveal the conformational rearrangements responsible for this remarkable allostery.
evidence: This is the primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by crystallographic data in the manuscript.

claim: The structures of E. coli class Ia RNR with substrate/effector pairs reveal the conformational rearrangements responsible for allosteric specificity regulation.
source: Here, we have determined structures of Escherichia coli class Ia RNR with all four substrate/specificity effector-pairs bound (CDP/dATP, UDP/dATP, ADP/dGTP, GDP/TTP) that reveal the conformational rearrangements responsible for this remarkable allostery.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the structural data presented.

claim: RNR 'reads' the base of each effector and communicates substrate preference to the active site by forming differential hydrogen bonds.
source: These structures delineate how RNR 'reads' the base of each effector and communicates substrate preference to the active site by forming differential hydrogen bonds, thereby maintaining the proper balance of deoxynucleotides in the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: RNR maintains the proper balance of deoxynucleotides in the cell through allosteric specificity regulation.
source: These structures delineate how RNR 'reads' the base of each effector and communicates substrate preference to the active site by forming differential hydrogen bonds, thereby maintaining the proper balance of deoxynucleotides in the cell.
evidence: This is stated as the biological function of the allosteric mechanism.

claim: Three classes of RNRs are known, categorized by the cofactor they use to generate a protein radical required for catalysis.
source: Three classes of RNRs are known, categorized by the cofactor they use to generate a protein radical required for catalysis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The class Ia enzyme from Escherichia coli is the best characterized of all RNRs.
source: The best characterized of all RNRs is the class Ia enzyme from Escherichia coli that employs a di-iron-tyrosyl-radical cofactor to initiate chemistry and requires two dimeric protein subunits for enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: E. coli class Ia RNR employs a di-iron-tyrosyl-radical cofactor to initiate chemistry.
source: The best characterized of all RNRs is the class Ia enzyme from Escherichia coli that employs a di-iron-tyrosyl-radical cofactor to initiate chemistry and requires two dimeric protein subunits for enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of the enzyme.

claim: E. coli class Ia RNR requires two dimeric protein subunits for enzymatic activity.
source: The best characterized of all RNRs is the class Ia enzyme from Escherichia coli that employs a di-iron-tyrosyl-radical cofactor to initiate chemistry and requires two dimeric protein subunits for enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of the enzyme.

claim: The α2 subunit of E. coli class Ia RNR contains two (β/α)10 barrels.
source: The α2 subunit contains two (β/α)10 barrels, which house the active sites at the barrel centers (Eriksson et al., 1997; Uhlin and Eklund, 1994)
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural studies.

claim: The active sites of E. coli class Ia RNR α2 subunit are located at the centers of the (β/α)10 barrels.
source: The α2 subunit contains two (β/α)10 barrels, which house the active sites at the barrel centers (Eriksson et al., 1997; Uhlin and Eklund, 1994)
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural studies.

claim: The β2 subunit of E. coli class Ia RNR utilizes a largely helical secondary structure to house the radical cofactor.
source: the β2 subunit utilizes a largely helical secondary structure to house the radical cofactor (Sjöberg and Reichard, 1977)
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural studies.

claim: RNR uses multiple allosteric mechanisms to maintain balanced deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate (dNTP) pools required for accurate DNA replication.
source: As a central controller of nucleotide metabolism, RNR uses multiple allosteric mechanisms to maintain the balanced deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate (dNTP) pools that are required for accurate DNA replication.
evidence: This is stated as a known function of RNR.

claim: Allosteric activity regulation modulates the overall size of dNTP pools.
source: First, allosteric activity regulation modulates the overall size of dNTP pools.
evidence: This is stated as one of the allosteric mechanisms of RNR.

claim: ATP or dATP binding at an allosteric activity site leads to up-regulation or down-regulation of enzyme activity, respectively.
source: ATP or dATP binding at an allosteric activity site, found at the N-terminus of α2 (Figure 1D), leads to up-regulation or down-regulation of enzyme activity, respectively (Brown and Reichard, 1969).
evidence: This is stated based on prior biochemical studies.

claim: The allosteric activity site is found at the N-terminus of α2.
source: ATP or dATP binding at an allosteric activity site, found at the N-terminus of α2 (Figure 1D), leads to up-regulation or down-regulation of enzyme activity, respectively (Brown and Reichard, 1969).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In E. coli class Ia RNR, allosteric activity regulation is achieved by changes in the oligomeric arrangement of the α2 and β2 subunits.
source: In E. coli class Ia RNR, this regulation is achieved by changes in the oligomeric arrangement of the α2 and β2 subunits (Brown and Reichard, 1969; Rofougaran et al., 2008; Ando et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on prior studies.

claim: When ATP is bound at the activity site, an α2β2 complex is favored.
source: When ATP is bound at the activity site, an α2β2 complex is favored.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of the enzyme.

claim: No X-ray structure of the active α2β2 complex has been determined.
source: Although no X-ray structure of the active complex has been determined, low resolution models have been generated using small-angle X-ray scattering (Ando et al., 2011), electron microscopy (Minnihan et al., 2013), and distance measurements made through spectroscopic analyses (Seyedsayamdost et al., 2007) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current structural knowledge.

claim: Low resolution models of the active α2β2 complex have been generated using small-angle X-ray scattering, electron microscopy, and spectroscopic analyses.
source: Although no X-ray structure of the active complex has been determined, low resolution models have been generated using small-angle X-ray scattering (Ando et al., 2011), electron microscopy (Minnihan et al., 2013), and distance measurements made through spectroscopic analyses (Seyedsayamdost et al., 2007) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated based on prior studies.

claim: The active α2β2 complex is capable of a long-range proton coupled electron transfer from β2 to α2.
source: This active α2β2 complex is capable of a long-range proton coupled electron transfer from β2 to α2, forming a transient thiyl radical on Cys439 to initiate catalysis (Licht et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated based on prior mechanistic studies.

claim: The active α2β2 complex forms a transient thiyl radical on Cys439 to initiate catalysis.
source: This active α2β2 complex is capable of a long-range proton coupled electron transfer from β2 to α2, forming a transient thiyl radical on Cys439 to initiate catalysis (Licht et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated based on prior mechanistic studies.

claim: When concentrations of dATP become too high in the cell, dATP binds at the allosteric activity site and formation of an α4β4 complex is promoted.
source: Alternatively, when concentrations of dATP become too high in the cell, dATP binds at the allosteric activity site and formation of an α4β4 complex is promoted.
evidence: This is stated as a known regulatory mechanism.

claim: The structure of the α4β4 complex was recently solved.
source: The structure of this complex was recently solved (Ando et al., 2011), revealing a ring of alternating α2 and β2 units that cannot form a productive electron transfer path, thus inhibiting the enzyme (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated based on a prior structural study.

claim: The α4β4 complex reveals a ring of alternating α2 and β2 units.
source: The structure of this complex was recently solved (Ando et al., 2011), revealing a ring of alternating α2 and β2 units that cannot form a productive electron transfer path, thus inhibiting the enzyme (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated based on a prior structural study and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The α4β4 complex cannot form a productive electron transfer path, thus inhibiting the enzyme.
source: The structure of this complex was recently solved (Ando et al., 2011), revealing a ring of alternating α2 and β2 units that cannot form a productive electron transfer path, thus inhibiting the enzyme (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated based on a prior structural study.

claim: Allosteric specificity regulation maintains the proper relative ratios of dNTPs in the cell.
source: The second form of allosteric regulation is specificity regulation, which maintains the proper relative ratios of dNTPs in the cell.
evidence: This is stated as one of the allosteric mechanisms of RNR.

claim: The binding of (d)NTP effectors to an allosteric specificity site in α2 influences the preference of RNR for its four nucleoside diphosphate (NDP) substrates.
source: Briefly, the binding of (d)NTP effectors to an allosteric specificity site in α2 influences the preference of RNR for its four nucleoside diphosphate (NDP) substrates.
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism of specificity regulation.

claim: At lower levels, dATP promotes CDP or UDP reduction.
source: Whereas high levels of dATP inhibit class Ia RNR, at lower levels, dATP promotes CDP or UDP reduction.
evidence: This is stated based on prior biochemical studies.

claim: TTP promotes GDP reduction.
source: Likewise, TTP promotes GDP reduction, and dGTP promotes ADP reduction (Figure 1E) (Brown and Reichard, 1969; Rofougaran et al., 2008; von Döbeln and Reichard, 1976).
evidence: This is stated based on prior biochemical studies.

claim: dGTP promotes ADP reduction.
source: Likewise, TTP promotes GDP reduction, and dGTP promotes ADP reduction (Figure 1E) (Brown and Reichard, 1969; Rofougaran et al., 2008; von Döbeln and Reichard, 1976).
evidence: This is stated based on prior biochemical studies.

claim: The affinity of the α2 and β2 subunits for each other is weak (~0.4 μM) in the absence of effectors.
source: Importantly, the affinity of the α2 and β2 subunits for each other is weak (~0.4 μM) in the absence of effectors, whereas the binding of a complementary substrate/specificity effector pair increases the affinity of the class Ia RNR subunits fivefold (Crona et al., 2010; Hassan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on prior biochemical studies.

claim: The binding of a complementary substrate/specificity effector pair increases the affinity of the class Ia RNR subunits fivefold.
source: Importantly, the affinity of the α2 and β2 subunits for each other is weak (~0.4 μM) in the absence of effectors, whereas the binding of a complementary substrate/specificity effector pair increases the affinity of the class Ia RNR subunits fivefold (Crona et al., 2010; Hassan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on prior biochemical studies.

claim: X-ray structures of GDP and TTP bound to E. coli α2 have been determined.
source: Previous structural work, which includes: X-ray structures of GDP and TTP bound to E. coli α2 (Eriksson et al., 1997), structures of all four substrate/effector pairs bound to class Ia α2 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Xu et al., 2006), and class II α2 from Thermotoga maritima (Larsson et al., 2004), revealed the location of the allosteric specificity sites at the ends of a four helix bundle at the dimer interface (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural studies.

claim: Structures of all four substrate/effector pairs bound to class Ia α2 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae have been determined.
source: Previous structural work, which includes: X-ray structures of GDP and TTP bound to E. coli α2 (Eriksson et al., 1997), structures of all four substrate/effector pairs bound to class Ia α2 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Xu et al., 2006), and class II α2 from Thermotoga maritima (Larsson et al., 2004), revealed the location of the allosteric specificity sites at the ends of a four helix bundle at the dimer interface (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural studies.

claim: Structures of all four substrate/effector pairs bound to class II α2 from Thermotoga maritima have been determined.
source: Previous structural work, which includes: X-ray structures of GDP and TTP bound to E. coli α2 (Eriksson et al., 1997), structures of all four substrate/effector pairs bound to class Ia α2 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Xu et al., 2006), and class II α2 from Thermotoga maritima (Larsson et al., 2004), revealed the location of the allosteric specificity sites at the ends of a four helix bundle at the dimer interface (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural studies.

claim: The allosteric specificity sites are located at the ends of a four helix bundle at the dimer interface.
source: Previous structural work, which includes: X-ray structures of GDP and TTP bound to E. coli α2 (Eriksson et al., 1997), structures of all four substrate/effector pairs bound to class Ia α2 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Xu et al., 2006), and class II α2 from Thermotoga maritima (Larsson et al., 2004), revealed the location of the allosteric specificity sites at the ends of a four helix bundle at the dimer interface (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural studies and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gln294 and Arg298 (E. coli numbering) are involved in the communication between the specificity site and the active site.
source: These data, and accompanying in vitro and in vivo studies on S. cerevisiae (Ahmad et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2011), also implicated which residues (Gln294 and Arg298, E. coli numbering) and which regions of the structure are involved in the communication between the specificity site and the active site.
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Loop 2 (residues 292–301 in E. coli) bridges the specificity site and the active site, which are approximately 15 Å apart.
source: A flexible loop, termed loop 2 (residues 292–301 in E. coli) (Figure 1B), bridges the two sites, which are approximately 15 Å apart, and becomes more ordered upon effector and substrate binding (Eriksson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural studies.

claim: Loop 2 becomes more ordered upon effector and substrate binding.
source: A flexible loop, termed loop 2 (residues 292–301 in E. coli) (Figure 1B), bridges the two sites, which are approximately 15 Å apart, and becomes more ordered upon effector and substrate binding (Eriksson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural studies.

claim: Loop 1 (residues 259–278) is near the effector-binding site and is stabilized upon effector binding.
source: An additional loop, termed loop 1 (residues 259–278), is also near the effector-binding site and is stabilized upon effector binding (Eriksson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated based on prior structural studies.

claim: An α4β4 crystal form of the E. coli class Ia RNR was utilized to obtain structures of all four substrate/specificity effector pairs.
source: We have utilized an α4β4 crystal form of the E. coli class Ia RNR (Figure 1D, right) (Ando et al., 2011; Zimanyi et al., 2012) to obtain structures of all four substrate/specificity effector pairs (CDP/dATP, UDP/dATP, ADP/dGTP or GDP/TTP) bound to the α2 subunit (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated as the method used in this study.

claim: Each model consists of two α2 dimers, two β2 dimers, and activity effector dATP in all four allosteric activity sites.
source: Each model consists of two α2 dimers, two β2 dimers, and activity effector dATP in all four allosteric activity sites.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the crystal structures.

claim: The α4β4 form of the enzyme cannot turn over substrates due to abrogation of the radical transfer pathway.
source: Although the α4β4 form of the enzyme cannot turn over substrates due to abrogation of the radical transfer pathway, the substrate and effector binding sites are not affected (Video 1).
evidence: This is stated as a property of the α4β4 complex.

claim: The substrate and effector binding sites are not affected in the α4β4 form of the enzyme.
source: Although the α4β4 form of the enzyme cannot turn over substrates due to abrogation of the radical transfer pathway, the substrate and effector binding sites are not affected (Video 1).
evidence: This is stated as a justification for using the α4β4 crystal form.

claim: In all structures, substrates and effectors were found ordered at their respective binding sites.
source: In all structures, substrates and effectors were found ordered at their respective binding sites (loop 2 electron density shown in Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Substrate/effector binding induces a closing of the (β/α)10 barrel around the bound substrate.
source: Each substrate/effector bound α4β4 structure reveals a closing of the (β/α)10 barrel around the bound substrate that is not observed in the absence of substrate.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing substrate-bound and substrate-free structures.

claim: The closing of the (β/α)10 barrel is not observed in the absence of substrate.
source: Each substrate/effector bound α4β4 structure reveals a closing of the (β/α)10 barrel around the bound substrate that is not observed in the absence of substrate.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing substrate-bound and substrate-free structures.

claim: One half of the active site barrel overlays exactly between substrate-bound and substrate-free structures when aligned by the finger loop, whereas the second half of the barrel and the N-terminal portion of the structure has undergone a clamping movement.
source: In this structural alignment, one half of the active site barrel overlays exactly, whereas the second half of the barrel and the N-terminal portion of the structure has undergone a clamping movement (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from structural superposition and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The N-terminal 220 residues shift substantially (>3Å), bringing them closer to half of the active site barrel (residues ~224–439).
source: The pattern of movements seen in the plot indicates that the N-terminal 220 residues (region 1 of Figure 3B,C) shift substantially (>3Å), bringing them closer to half of the active site barrel (residues ~224–439, region 2 of Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the difference distance matrix analysis and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Loop 2 and a flexible β hairpin (residues 646–651) undergo substantial motions upon substrate/effector binding.
source: We also observe that loop 2 (region 3 of Figure 3B,C) and a flexible β hairpin that sits adjacent to the N-terminus (residues 646–651, region 5 of Figure 3B,C) undergo substantial motions.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the difference distance matrix analysis and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Residues Ser622, Ser625, and Thr209 form hydrogen bonds with the NDP substrate.
source: Residues Ser622, Ser625, and Thr209 form hydrogen bonds with the NDP substrate, whereas in the substrate-free state (pink ribbon in Figure 4A), these residues are shifted away from the center of the barrel.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the substrate-free state, Ser622, Ser625, and Thr209 are shifted away from the center of the barrel.
source: Residues Ser622, Ser625, and Thr209 form hydrogen bonds with the NDP substrate, whereas in the substrate-free state (pink ribbon in Figure 4A), these residues are shifted away from the center of the barrel.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing substrate-bound and substrate-free structures and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Thr209 is part of the N-terminal region that moves upon substrate binding.
source: Thr209 is part of the N-terminal region that is shown to move in the DDM analysis.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: Loop 2 shifts, bringing Arg298 closer to the active site upon substrate/effector binding.
source: The structure superposition and DDM analysis also indicate that loop 2 shifts, bringing Arg298 closer to the active site.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: The Arg298 side chain forms a cation-π interaction with the substrate base and a charge-charge interaction with the substrate β-phosphate.
source: The Arg298 side chain now forms a cation-π interaction with the substrate base and a charge-charge interaction with the substrate β-phosphate.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: In the substrate-free structure, the Arg298 side chain is pointing in the opposite direction.
source: In the substrate-free structure, this side chain is pointing in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing substrate-bound and substrate-free structures.

claim: Protein contacts like Arg298 to the substrate diphosphate are expected to be particularly important for charge neutralization in enzymes that do not employ metal cations such as Mg2+ for this purpose.
source: Protein contacts like Arg298 to the substrate diphosphate are expected to be particularly important for charge neutralization in enzymes, such as E. coli RNR, that do not employ metal cations such as Mg2+ for this purpose.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on chemical principles.

claim: The positions of residues that contact the ribose O3' (Glu441 and Asn437) are virtually unchanged between the NDP-free and NDP-bound structures.
source: The positions of residues that contact the ribose O3' (Glu441 and Asn437) are virtually unchanged between the NDP-free and NDP-bound structures (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing structures and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All four substrate-bound structures show almost identical contacts between the enzyme and the substrate ribose and phosphates.
source: All four of our substrate-bound structures show almost identical contacts between the enzyme and the substrate ribose and phosphates as described here and shown in Figure 4A,C and Figure 5 for GDP and CDP, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: In a previously reported α2 structure with GDP bound at an occupancy of 0.5, Ser622, Ser625 and Thr209 are all 3.0 Å or greater from the substrate diphosphate.
source: In this structure, Ser622, Ser625, and Thr209 are all 3.0 Å or greater from the substrate diphosphate, and Arg298 points away from the active site (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from a previously reported structure and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In a previously reported α2 structure with GDP bound at an occupancy of 0.5, Arg298 points away from the active site.
source: In this structure, Ser622, Ser625, and Thr209 are all 3.0 Å or greater from the substrate diphosphate, and Arg298 points away from the active site (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from a previously reported structure and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Weaker interactions between protein and substrate in the previously determined α2 structure are consistent with substrate being observed in an altered orientation in the active site and present at only half occupancy.
source: These weaker (or missing) interactions between protein and substrate in this previously determined structure are consistent with the fact that substrate is observed in an altered orientation in the active site (Figure 4C,D) and is only present at half occupancy.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from comparing structures and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The differences in substrate positioning in the previously determined α2 structure are attributed to the inability of the active site barrel to clamp around substrate due to crystal lattice contacts.
source: We attribute the differences in substrate positioning in this structure to the inability of the active site barrel to clamp around substrate due to crystal lattice contacts.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the structural differences.

claim: Symmetry-related molecules are closer to the active site in the α2-only crystalline state than they are in the α4β4 crystal form.
source: Symmetry-related molecules are closer to the active site in the α2-only crystalline state than they are in the α4β4 crystal form.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing crystal packing.

claim: Differences in flexibility between α4β4 and α2 cannot be attributed to the fact that α4β4 is an inactive state because α2 is also an inactive state.
source: Importantly, differences in flexibility cannot be attributed to the fact that α4β4 is an inactive state of E. coli RNR because α2 is also an inactive state; the former because β2 is held at arm's length from α2, and the latter because β2 is absent altogether.
evidence: This is stated as a justification for comparing the two crystal forms.

claim: α2 should be able to clamp in the presence of a cognate substrate/effector pair regardless of β2 when lattice contacts do not restrain α2 movement.
source: When lattice contacts do not restrain α2 movement, α2 should be able to clamp in the presence of a cognate substrate/effector pair regardless of β2.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: Different crystal forms have given two distinct snapshots of substrate-bound states for the E. coli class Ia enzyme: a high affinity state which is closed and ready for radical-based chemistry when β2 becomes available and a lower affinity state in which substrate is still exposed to solvent and not ready to undergo catalysis.
source: Thus, it seems that different crystal forms have given us two distinct snapshots of substrate-bound states for the E. coli class Ia enzyme: a high affinity state which is closed and ready for radical-based chemistry when β2 becomes available (Figure 4C) and a lower affinity state in which substrate is still exposed to solvent and not ready to undergo catalysis, regardless of the availability of β2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing the two crystal forms and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Regardless of the identity of the dNTP base, the ribose and phosphates of the three specificity effectors (dATP, dGTP, and TTP) form almost identical contacts with RNR.
source: Regardless of the identity of the dNTP base, the ribose and phosphates of the three specificity effectors (dATP, dGTP, and TTP) form almost identical contacts with RNR (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The common interactions between specificity effectors and RNR are made with only one chain of the α2 dimer.
source: Despite the presence of the specificity effector site at the dimer interface, these common interactions are made with only one chain of the α2 dimer.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: Asp232 and His275 are within hydrogen-bonding distance of O3' of the ribose of specificity effectors.
source: Asp232 and His275 are within hydrogen-bonding distance of O3' of the ribose.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: One Mg2+ ion appears to form an octahedral coordination complex with three phosphate oxygens of the specificity effector and three water molecules.
source: One Mg2+ ion appears to form an octahedral coordination complex with three phosphate oxygens of the specificity effector and three water molecules (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 6.

claim: There are hydrogen bonds between the phosphates of specificity effectors and the backbone amides of residues Arg269 and Leu234.
source: There are also hydrogen bonds between the phosphates and the backbone amides of residues Arg269 and Leu234 and charge-charge interactions with the side chains of Arg269 and/or Arg262.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: There are charge-charge interactions between the phosphates of specificity effectors and the side chains of Arg269 and/or Arg262.
source: There are also hydrogen bonds between the phosphates and the backbone amides of residues Arg269 and Leu234 and charge-charge interactions with the side chains of Arg269 and/or Arg262.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: Loop 2 is ordered in all four structures.
source: Loop 2 is ordered in all four structures as indicated by 2Fo–Fc composite omit electron density (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Arg298 of loop 2 forms a conserved interaction with the β-phosphate of all four substrates.
source: As noted above, Arg298 of loop 2 forms a conserved interaction with the β-phosphate of all four substrates (Figures 7, 8).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Cys292 packs against the base of all three effectors.
source: On the effector side of loop 2, Cys292 packs against the base of all three effectors (Figures 7, 8), consistent with binding studies that show the affinity for all specificity effectors is decreased when Cys292 is mutated to alanine (Ormö and Sjöberg, 1996).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The affinity for all specificity effectors is decreased when Cys292 is mutated to alanine.
source: On the effector side of loop 2, Cys292 packs against the base of all three effectors (Figures 7, 8), consistent with binding studies that show the affinity for all specificity effectors is decreased when Cys292 is mutated to alanine (Ormö and Sjöberg, 1996).
evidence: This is stated based on prior biochemical studies.

claim: dATP makes two hydrogen bonds with loop 2 through the backbone amide and carbonyl of Ser293 to N1 and N6 of the adenine base.
source: The backbone amide and carbonyl of Ser293 are in position to hydrogen bond to N1 and N6, respectively, of the adenine base of dATP.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: The hydrogen bonds between Ser293 and dATP hold Ser293 in place and position the adjacent Gln294 in a conformation that points into the substrate-binding site.
source: These hydrogen bonds hold Ser293 in place and position the adjacent Gln294 in to a conformation that points into the substrate-binding site (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 8.

claim: In the dATP-bound conformation, Gln294 can form a hydrogen bond with O2 of CDP or UDP.
source: In this conformation, Gln294 can form a hydrogen bond with O2 of CDP or UDP.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: There is no difference in substrate positioning between CDP and UDP.
source: There is no difference in substrate positioning between CDP and UDP, as the unique positions of the pyrimidine ring (N2 and N4/O4) are not involved in any contacts with the protein.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: The positioning of Gln294 by dATP selects for pyrimidine binding, as binding of a purine base would be disfavored due to steric occlusion by Gln294.
source: Furthermore, the positioning of Gln294 by dATP selects for pyrimidine binding, as binding of a purine base would be disfavored due to steric occlusion by Gln294.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: dGTP forms one hydrogen bond with loop 1 residue Thr276 in addition to its loop 2 contacts.
source: dGTP, which preferentially increases RNR activity for substrate ADP, forms one hydrogen bond with loop 1 residue Thr276 (Figure 6C) in addition to its loop 2 contacts.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: dGTP is the only effector for which a hydrogen bond is formed between the base and loop 1.
source: It is the only effector for which a hydrogen bond is formed between the base and loop 1.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing all four structures.

claim: Because the position of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors at N1 and O6 in dGTP is opposite from that of N1 and N6 of dATP, the interaction with the backbone amide of Ser293 in loop 2 is unfavorable in the dGTP-bound structure.
source: Because the position of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors at N1 and O6 in dGTP is opposite from that of N1 and N6 of dATP, the interaction with the backbone amide of Ser293 in loop 2 is unfavorable in this structure.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on chemical principles and structural observations.

claim: In the dGTP-bound structure, Ser293 is shifted away from the base, and N1 and N2 of dGTP form an interaction with the backbone carbonyl of Gln294, which has shifted away from the substrate.
source: Instead, Ser293 is shifted away from the base, and N1 and N2 – both hydrogen bond donors – form an interaction with the backbone carbonyl of Gln294, which has shifted away from the substrate (Figure 7A–C and 8A–C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: In the dGTP-bound structure, Ser293 makes no hydrogen bond contacts to dGTP and instead provides hydrogen bonds to Gly300 on the other side of loop 2 through both its side chain and backbone.
source: Ser293 thus makes no hydrogen bond contacts to dGTP and instead provides hydrogen bonds to Gly300 on the other side of loop 2 through both its side chain and backbone.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: Stabilization of Gly300 in the dGTP-bound conformation allows for a hydrogen bond between the carbonyl of Gly299 with the N6 position of the preferred substrate, ADP.
source: Stabilization of Gly300 in this position in turn allows for a hydrogen bond between the carbonyl of Gly299 with the N6 position of the preferred substrate, ADP.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: The movement of Gln294 away from the substrate-binding site allows room for the larger ADP to bind.
source: The movement of Gln294 away from the substrate-binding site allows room for the larger ADP to bind.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: Ser293 and Gln294 are responsible both for differentiating between the purine bases adenine and guanine at the effector-binding site and for differentiating pyrimidines from purines at the substrate site.
source: Thus, Ser293 and Gln294 are responsible both for differentiating between the purine bases adenine and guanine at the effector-binding site and for differentiating pyrimidines from purines at the substrate site, either directly (in the case of Gln294 hydrogen bonding to CDP or UDP) or indirectly through stabilization of Gly299 and Gly300.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: With dATP bound, Ser293 plays a role in effector recognition and Gln294 in substrate recognition.
source: With dATP bound, Ser293 plays a role in effector recognition and Gln294 in substrate recognition; these roles are reversed for ADP/dGTP.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: With dGTP bound, the roles of Ser293 and Gln294 are reversed compared to dATP binding.
source: With dATP bound, Ser293 plays a role in effector recognition and Gln294 in substrate recognition; these roles are reversed for ADP/dGTP.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: TTP binds to the specificity site such that only the carbonyl of Cys292 from loop 2 is positioned to form a hydrogen-bonding interaction with the thymine base.
source: TTP, which preferentially increases RNR activity for substrate GDP, binds to the specificity site such that only the carbonyl of Cys292 from loop 2 is positioned to form a hydrogen-bonding interaction with the thymine base (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: In the GDP/TTP structure, Gln294 is swung away from the active site to make room for the binding of a purine substrate.
source: As in the ADP/dGTP structure, Gln294 is swung away from the active site to make room for the binding of a purine substrate (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: N1 and N2 of GDP are both within hydrogen-bonding distance of the backbone carbonyl of Gly299.
source: On the substrate side of loop 2, N1 and N2 of GDP are both within hydrogen-bonding distance of the backbone carbonyl of Gly299.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: N2 of GDP is also within hydrogen-bonding distance of the backbone carbonyl of Ala252.
source: N2 of GDP is also within hydrogen-bonding distance of the backbone carbonyl of Ala252 (not shown), giving GDP one more hydrogen bond than the other substrates
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: For the purine substrates ADP and GDP, preference appears to rely on a shift of the carbonyl of Gly299 in loop 2 forward or backward in the active site, enabled by the binding of dGTP or TTP, respectively, at the specificity site.
source: For the purine substrates ADP and GDP, preference appears to rely on a shift of the carbonyl of Gly299 in loop 2 forward or backward in the active site, enabled by the binding of dGTP or TTP, respectively, at the specificity site.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: With dGTP bound, Ser293 is positioned such that it pushes the carbonyl of Gly299 'forward' (away from the effector-side of loop 2), allowing a hydrogen bond to form between the carbonyl of Gly299 and N6 of adenine.
source: With dGTP bound, Ser293 is positioned such that it pushes the carbonyl of Gly299 'forward' (away from the effector-side of loop 2, see Figure 8C), allowing a hydrogen bond to form between the carbonyl of Gly299 and N6 of adenine.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: With TTP bound, Ser293 rearranges such that the carbonyl of Gly299 can relax 'backward' (toward the effector-side of loop 2), allowing for a hydrogen bond between the carbonyl of Gly299 and N1 and N2 of guanine.
source: With the smaller TTP in the effector site, Ser293 rearranges such that the carbonyl of Gly299 can relax 'backward' (toward the effector-side of loop 2, see Figure 8D), allowing for a hydrogen bond between the carbonyl of Gly299 and N1 and N2 of guanine.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Specificity for ADP versus GDP is imparted by the fact that the 'forward' position of the Gly299 carbonyl interacts with the 6-position of the purine, which is a hydrogen bond donor (NH2) in adenine and a hydrogen bond acceptor (O) in guanine.
source: Specificity is imparted by the fact that the 'forward' position of the Gly299 carbonyl interacts with the 6-position of the purine, which is a hydrogen bond donor (NH2) in adenine and a hydrogen bond acceptor (O) in guanine; and the 'backward' position of the Gly299 carbonyl interacts with the 1-position and 2-position of the purine, which are both hydrogen bond donors (NH and NH2) in guanine but not in adenine (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for specificity based on structural observations and shown in Figure 8.

claim: The 'backward' position of the Gly299 carbonyl interacts with the 1-position and 2-position of the purine, which are both hydrogen bond donors (NH and NH2) in guanine but not in adenine.
source: Specificity is imparted by the fact that the 'forward' position of the Gly299 carbonyl interacts with the 6-position of the purine, which is a hydrogen bond donor (NH2) in adenine and a hydrogen bond acceptor (O) in guanine; and the 'backward' position of the Gly299 carbonyl interacts with the 1-position and 2-position of the purine, which are both hydrogen bond donors (NH and NH2) in guanine but not in adenine (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for specificity based on structural observations and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Purines are favored over pyrimidines when Gln294 is positioned away from the active site creating a larger substrate-binding pocket.
source: To briefly summarize purine specificity, purines are favored over pyrimidines when Gln294 is positioned away from the active site creating a larger substrate-binding pocket, and ADP is favored over GDP when dGTP binding stabilizes Ser293 close to the Gly299 backbone pushing its carbonyl forward, and GDP is favored over ADP when TTP allows Ser293 to fall back.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the structural findings.

claim: ADP is favored over GDP when dGTP binding stabilizes Ser293 close to the Gly299 backbone pushing its carbonyl forward.
source: To briefly summarize purine specificity, purines are favored over pyrimidines when Gln294 is positioned away from the active site creating a larger substrate-binding pocket, and ADP is favored over GDP when dGTP binding stabilizes Ser293 close to the Gly299 backbone pushing its carbonyl forward, and GDP is favored over ADP when TTP allows Ser293 to fall back.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the structural findings.

claim: GDP is favored over ADP when TTP allows Ser293 to fall back.
source: To briefly summarize purine specificity, purines are favored over pyrimidines when Gln294 is positioned away from the active site creating a larger substrate-binding pocket, and ADP is favored over GDP when dGTP binding stabilizes Ser293 close to the Gly299 backbone pushing its carbonyl forward, and GDP is favored over ADP when TTP allows Ser293 to fall back.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the structural findings.

claim: Gln294Ala and Arg298Ala mutant enzymes were prepared and tested for activity with each substrate/effector pair.
source: To confirm this prediction, we prepared Gln294Ala and Arg298Ala mutant enzymes and tested the activity for each substrate/effector pair.
evidence: This is stated as a method used to test the structural predictions.

claim: Wild-type RNR is as active (CDP/dATP) or more active (UDP/dATP) at 1 μM dATP than it is in the positive control (CDP/ATP).
source: Results show that wild-type RNR is as active (CDP/dATP) or more active (UDP/dATP) at 1 μM dATP than it is in the positive control (CDP/ATP), indicating that at 1 μM, dATP is acting as a specificity effector and not as an allosteric inhibitor of activity, consistent with previous studies (Birgander et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the activity assays.

claim: At 1 μM, dATP is acting as a specificity effector and not as an allosteric inhibitor of activity.
source: Results show that wild-type RNR is as active (CDP/dATP) or more active (UDP/dATP) at 1 μM dATP than it is in the positive control (CDP/ATP), indicating that at 1 μM, dATP is acting as a specificity effector and not as an allosteric inhibitor of activity, consistent with previous studies (Birgander et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the activity assay results.

claim: At 175 μM dATP, wild-type RNR activity on CDP is substantially decreased.
source: The negative control shows the substantial decrease in wild-type RNR activity on CDP when the concentration of dATP is high enough (175 μM) for dATP to bind to the allosteric activity site and inhibit the enzyme.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the activity assays.

claim: Mutation of Arg298 to alanine should decrease activity for all substrates.
source: Our structures predict that mutation of Arg298 to alanine should decrease activity for all substrates, and that is exactly what we observe (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the structures that is confirmed by the activity assays and shown in Figure 9.

claim: Arg298Ala-RNR shows negligible activity for all substrate/effector pairs.
source: The effect is dramatic for this mutant, with negligible activity observed in all cases.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the activity assays.

claim: Arg298Ala-RNR is either mostly or completely inactive.
source: Thus, Arg298Ala-RNR is either mostly or completely inactive.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the activity assays.

claim: For Gln294Ala-RNR, minimal or no loss of activity on ADP/GDP is expected and measurable loss on CDP/UDP is expected.
source: In contrast, for Gln294Ala-RNR, we would expect purine and pyrimidine substrates to be differentially affected, with minimal or no loss of activity on ADP/GDP and measurable loss on CDP/UDP, and that is again what we observe.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the structures that is confirmed by the activity assays.

claim: For Gln294Ala, activity is the same as wild-type for ADP/dGTP and perhaps even higher than wild-type for GDP/TTP.
source: For Gln294Ala, activity is the same as wild-type for ADP/dGTP and perhaps even higher than wild-type for GDP/TTP, whereas for both CDP and UDP with 1 μM dATP, activity is decreased (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the activity assays and shown in Figure 9.

claim: For Gln294Ala, activity is decreased for both CDP and UDP with 1 μM dATP.
source: For Gln294Ala, activity is the same as wild-type for ADP/dGTP and perhaps even higher than wild-type for GDP/TTP, whereas for both CDP and UDP with 1 μM dATP, activity is decreased (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the activity assays and shown in Figure 9.

claim: The activity results for Gln294Ala are consistent with the removal of the Gln294 side chain from the active site to create room for the larger substrates (ADP/GDP) to bind.
source: These results are consistent with the removal of the Gln294 side chain from the active site to create room for the larger substrates (ADP/GDP) to bind and also with the positioning of Gln294 into the active site to stabilize CDP/UDP binding through hydrogen-bonding to the respective bases.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the activity assay results in light of the structural data.

claim: The activity results for Gln294Ala are consistent with the positioning of Gln294 into the active site to stabilize CDP/UDP binding through hydrogen-bonding to the respective bases.
source: These results are consistent with the removal of the Gln294 side chain from the active site to create room for the larger substrates (ADP/GDP) to bind and also with the positioning of Gln294 into the active site to stabilize CDP/UDP binding through hydrogen-bonding to the respective bases.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the activity assay results in light of the structural data.

claim: In the absence of substrates or effectors, the barrel is not clamped and loop 2 is not found in any of the conformations seen in the effector-bound structures.
source: We observe that in the absence of substrates or effectors (for example, in the previously reported structure of α2 (PDB ID: 3R1R (Eriksson et al., 1997)), the barrel is not clamped and loop 2 is not found in any of the conformations seen in our effector-bound structures (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing structures and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In the presence of substrate/effector pairs, a clamped down barrel and a stabilized loop 2 that adopts three different conformations depending on the allosteric effector that is bound are observed.
source: However, in the presence of substrate/effector pairs, we find a clamped down barrel and a stabilized loop 2 that adopts three different conformations depending on the allosteric effector that is bound (Figure 7A–D) (Video 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures and shown in Figure 7 and Video 2.

claim: Loop 2 residues Cys292, Ser293, and Gln294 appear to be involved in specific interactions that read out the identity of the base and communicate that identity to the active site.
source: Loop 2 residues Cys292, Ser293, and Gln294 appear to be involved in specific interactions that read out the identity of the base and communicate that identity to the active site.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: dATP makes specific contacts with Ser293, orienting Gln294 toward the active site and stabilizing the binding of both CDP and UDP.
source: Briefly, dATP, which enhances reduction of CDP/UDP (von Döbeln and Reichard, 1976), makes specific contacts with Ser293, orienting Gln294 toward the active site and stabilizing the binding of both CDP and UDP (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis and shown in Figure 8.

claim: The lack of discrimination between CDP and UDP substrates by RNR is not problematic for the cell as cytidine deaminase provides another level of control for dCTP/TTP ratios.
source: The lack of discrimination between CDP and UDP substrates by RNR is not problematic for the cell as cytidine deaminase provides another level of control for dCTP/TTP ratios (Wang and Weiss, 1992; O'Donovan et al., 1971).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation based on prior knowledge.

claim: dGTP binding stabilizes Gln294 away from the RNR active site, so that CDP/UDP binding is not stabilized and there is room for the larger purine substrates to bind and to hydrogen bond to the carbonyl of Gly299.
source: In contrast, dGTP binding stabilizes Gln294 away from the RNR active site, so that CDP/UDP binding is not stabilized (although it is not prohibited) and there is room for the larger purine substrates to bind and to hydrogen bond to the carbonyl of Gly299 (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis and shown in Figure 8.

claim: The creation of a more expansive active site by dGTP binding is consistent with the ability of RNR to reduce both purine substrates in the presence of dGTPγS, albeit with a much greater fold activity increase for preferred substrate ADP.
source: The creation of a more expansive active site is consistent with the ability of RNR to reduce both purine substrates in the presence of dGTPγS, albeit with a much greater fold activity increase for preferred substrate ADP (von Döbeln and Reichard, 1976).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the structural findings in light of prior biochemical data.

claim: Movement of Gln294 in and out of the active site alternatively shrinks and expands the active site for CDP/UDP versus ADP/GDP.
source: Thus, our structural data suggest that movement of Gln294 in and out of the active site alternatively shrinks and expands the active site for CDP/UDP versus ADP/GDP, whereas a more modest shift of the Gly299 carbonyl is involved in ADP/GDP selectivity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: A more modest shift of the Gly299 carbonyl is involved in ADP/GDP selectivity.
source: Thus, our structural data suggest that movement of Gln294 in and out of the active site alternatively shrinks and expands the active site for CDP/UDP versus ADP/GDP, whereas a more modest shift of the Gly299 carbonyl is involved in ADP/GDP selectivity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: Mutagenesis of Gln294 to Ala shows decreased activity on CDP/UDP and no change or increased activity on ADP/GDP.
source: Mutagenesis of Gln294 to Ala is consistent with this proposal, showing decreased activity on CDP/UDP and no change or increased activity on ADP/GDP (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the activity assays that supports the structural conclusions and shown in Figure 9.

claim: When a cognate substrate/effector pair is bound and the barrel is clamped, Arg298 is able to reach across the active site, stack against the NDP base, and hydrogen bond to the NDP β-phosphate.
source: When a cognate substrate/effector pair is bound and the barrel is clamped, Arg298 is able to reach across the active site, stack against the NDP base, and hydrogen bond to the NDP β-phosphate, thereby sequestering the substrate in the active site, and neutralizing the substrate negative charge.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: Arg298 sequesters the substrate in the active site and neutralizes the substrate negative charge.
source: When a cognate substrate/effector pair is bound and the barrel is clamped, Arg298 is able to reach across the active site, stack against the NDP base, and hydrogen bond to the NDP β-phosphate, thereby sequestering the substrate in the active site, and neutralizing the substrate negative charge.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: The interactions of Arg298 with substrate yield a high affinity substrate-bound state that is sequestered from solvent and thus amenable to radical-based chemistry.
source: These interactions yield what appears to be a high affinity substrate-bound state that is sequestered by solvent and thus amenable to radical-based chemistry.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: Arg298 is like a latch on a suitcase, locking the active site barrel when the active site is appropriately packed.
source: To invoke an analogy, Arg298 is like a latch on a suitcase, locking the active site barrel in cases in which the active site is appropriately packed (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is stated as an analogy to explain the function of Arg298 and shown in Figure 10A.

claim: A mismatched substrate/effector pair such as a purine nucleotide with dATP would not be expected to allow the barrel to clamp and loop 2 to rearrange such that Arg298 can reach the substrate phosphate.
source: Similarly, a mismatched substrate/effector pair such as a purine nucleotide with dATP would not be expected to allow the barrel to clamp and loop 2 to rearrange such that Arg298 can reach the substrate phosphate and thus form a 'latched' complex (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural observations and shown in Figure 10B.

claim: A mismatched substrate would be expected to be released from the enzyme, so that a complementary one can bind.
source: In the latter case, one would expect the mismatched substrate to be released from the enzyme, so that a complementary one can bind.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: Allosteric regulation of specificity would require both low and high affinity substrate/effector-enzyme states.
source: Chemical logic tells us that allosteric regulation of specificity would require both low and high affinity substrate/effector-enzyme states; low affinity states to sample substrate/effector pairs, and high affinity states to capture the correct pair, recruit β2 (class I) or adenosylcobalamin (class II), and initiate catalysis (Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about the mechanism of allosteric regulation and shown in Figure 10.

claim: The molecular basis for the fivefold increase in binding affinity of β2 for α2 in E. coli class Ia RNR in the presence of bound substrate/effector pairs is not understood.
source: Although the molecular basis for the fivefold increase in binding affinity of β2 for α2 in E. coli class Ia RNR in the presence of bound substrate/effector pairs is not understood, the clamping of the barrel that we observe here may be part of the molecular explanation.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current understanding.

claim: The clamping of the barrel may be part of the molecular explanation for the fivefold increase in binding affinity of β2 for α2 in the presence of bound substrate/effector pairs.
source: Although the molecular basis for the fivefold increase in binding affinity of β2 for α2 in E. coli class Ia RNR in the presence of bound substrate/effector pairs is not understood, the clamping of the barrel that we observe here may be part of the molecular explanation.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: The use of Arg298 as a molecular latch to secure the barrel in the closed state is consistent with both structural and biochemical data that show almost complete loss of activity in the Arg298Ala variant.
source: The use of Arg298 as a molecular latch to secure the barrel in this closed state is beautiful in its simplicity. It is also consistent with both our structural and our biochemical data that show almost complete loss of activity in the Arg298Ala variant (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural and biochemical data and shown in Figure 9.

claim: Loop 2 is not highly conserved, even among characterized RNRs.
source: Loop 2 is clearly an important player in specificity regulation, and yet it is not highly conserved, even among characterized RNRs (Figure 11).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from sequence alignments and shown in Figure 11.

claim: Backbone atoms of loop 2 make the vast majority of contacts to the substrate base and the effector base.
source: This being said, our structures show that backbone atoms of loop 2 make the vast majority of contacts to the substrate base and the effector base, limiting the number of residues that need to be strictly conserved to allow for the same molecular mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: Despite fairly low sequence identities between the E. coli and the T. maritima α subunits (20.5%) and the E. coli and the S. cerevisiae α subunits (29.3%), all three enzymes interact with the phosphate groups and ribose moieties of their substrates and effectors in similar ways.
source: Also, despite the fairly low sequence identities between the E. coli and the T. maritima α subunits (20.5%) and the E. coli and the S. cerevisiae α subunits (29.3%), a structural comparison shows that all three enzymes interact with the phosphate groups and ribose moieties of their substrates and effectors in similar ways (Table 4).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from structural comparisons and shown in Table 4.

claim: In E. coli, Arg298 directly contacts the β-phosphate of all four substrates.
source: The only noteworthy difference is that Arg298, critical for reduction of all four NDPs in E. coli, directly contacts the β-phosphate of all four substrates.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: None of the four S. cerevisiae RNR structures show a direct contact to the β-phosphate by the equivalent arginine.
source: In contrast, none of the four S. cerevisiae RNR structures show a direct contact to the β-phosphate by the equivalent arginine, although one structure shows a through-water contact, and only one of the substrate/effector bound structures of T. maritima RNR (GDP/TTP) shows direct contact.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing structures.

claim: Only one of the substrate/effector bound structures of T. maritima RNR (GDP/TTP) shows direct contact between the equivalent arginine and the substrate β-phosphate.
source: In contrast, none of the four S. cerevisiae RNR structures show a direct contact to the β-phosphate by the equivalent arginine, although one structure shows a through-water contact, and only one of the substrate/effector bound structures of T. maritima RNR (GDP/TTP) shows direct contact.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing structures.

claim: The GDP/TTP-bound structure of T. maritima RNR is the only T. maritima RNR structure in which loop 2 is fully ordered.
source: This GDP/TTP-bound structure is the only T. maritima RNR structure in which loop 2 is fully ordered and it is remarkably similar to our E. coli structures (Figure 10H,I).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing structures and shown in Figure 10.

claim: The GDP/TTP-bound structure of T. maritima RNR is remarkably similar to the E. coli structures.
source: This GDP/TTP-bound structure is the only T. maritima RNR structure in which loop 2 is fully ordered and it is remarkably similar to our E. coli structures (Figure 10H,I).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing structures and shown in Figure 10.

claim: All contacts made to GDP are the same between E. coli and T. maritima RNR: Arg side chain to β-phosphate, and loop 2 carbonyl to N1 and N2 of base.
source: All contacts made to GDP are the same: Arg side chain to β-phosphate, and loop 2 carbonyl to N1 and N2 of base (Figure 10H, 4C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing structures and shown in Figure 10 and Figure 4C.

claim: The TTP contacts are not identical between E. coli and T. maritima RNR, but in both cases, the resulting loop 2 conformations allow the carbonyl of 299 (E. coli numbering) and 208 (T. maritima numbering) to 'fall back' to contact N1 and N2 of GDP.
source: The TTP contacts are not identical, but in both cases, the resulting loop 2 conformations allow the carbonyl of 299 (E. coli numbering) and 208 (T. maritima numbering) to 'fall back' to contact N1 and N2 of GDP.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing structures.

claim: The T. maritima class II RNR structures reveal a movement of Gln294 in and out of the active site in response to effector binding.
source: Excitingly, the T. maritima class II RNR structures also reveal a movement of Gln294 in and out of the active site in response to effector binding.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior structural studies.

claim: In the GDP/TTP and CDP/dATP bound structures from T. maritima class II RNR, Gln203 (equivalent to Gln294 in E. coli) interacts directly with CDP when dATP is bound, and moves away from the active site when GDP/TTP are bound.
source: In particular, the GDP/TTP and CDP/dATP bound structures from T. maritima class II RNR, which have an ordered and semi-ordered loop 2, respectively, show that Gln203 (equivalent to Gln294 in E. coli) interacts directly with CDP when dATP is bound, and moves away from the active site when GDP/TTP are bound (Larsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior structural studies.

claim: Many loop 2 residues are disordered and thus not modeled in the T. maritima structures with CDP/dATP, UDP/dATP, and ADP/dGTP.
source: Unfortunately, many loop 2 residues are disordered and thus not modeled in the T. maritima structures with CDP/dATP, UDP/dATP, and ADP/dGTP, preventing further comparison to our E. coli structures.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the prior structural studies.

claim: Gln288 in S. cerevisiae class Ia RNR is observed to point into the active site in all structures, regardless of which substrate/effector pairs are bound.
source: In stark contrast to the behavior of Gln294 in E. coli and Gln203 in T. maritima, Gln288 in S. cerevisiae class Ia RNR is observed to point into the active site in all structures, regardless of which substrate/effector pairs are bound.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior structural studies.

claim: The protein does not pack as tightly around purine substrates when Gln points into the active site as it does when Gln is flipped away.
source: Structural comparisons show that the protein does not pack as tightly around purine substrates when Gln points into the active site as it does when Gln is flipped away (Figure 10E,F compared with 10H,I).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing structures and shown in Figure 10.

claim: It is possible that the difference in Gln positioning in S. cerevisiae indicates that the mechanism of allosteric regulation is not conserved among RNRs.
source: It is possible that this difference in Gln positioning in S. cerevisiae, and differences described above for Arg298 (E. coli numbering), indicate that the mechanism of allosteric regulation is not conserved among RNRs.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about the conservation of mechanism.
